text: Disease-causing fungi are multi-cellular, made of microscopic filaments, and become visible under a microscope when grown on culture media (about 0.005 mm — 5 times bigger than bacteria). Fungi are everywhere and animals are constantly exposed to them; under normal conditions animals develop protection against fungi, and disease generally only develops alongside general weakness, other illness, or low immunity. The best-known disease-causing fungi, Aspergillus, affect animal health in two main ways: through mycotoxin production (aflatoxin, found in moldy raw materials — especially corn — causes liver damage with regular intake and destroys immunity), and through infection, either localized (e.g. ringworm, a fungal skin infection in pigs or cattle) or systemic (e.g. Aspergillosis in chicks, a general disease following inhalation of fungal spores).
